title: Referral incentives that respect consumer and spam rules
audience: Any home-service operator who wants existing customers to refer new ones, and who must do so within consumer and messaging rules.
learningOutcomes: Write a referral reward with clear conditions, a cap and a payment trigger
Identify the consumer and messaging checks that apply before a referral message is sent
Calculate the cost of a referral reward per referred paying customer

instruction.heading: Why referrals work and where they fail
instruction.body: A referral incentive asks an existing customer to bring in someone they know, in return for a reward. The sample plan this lesson draws on argued that a financial reward would motivate that behaviour, and that people like to pass on a good deal to friends. That is a reasonable starting point. Referral schemes fail when the terms are vague, when the reward is paid before any real work is done, or when the business sends messages to people who never agreed to hear from it.

instruction.heading: Design the reward on paper first
instruction.body: Write three things before the scheme is announced: the reward, the trigger and the cap. The reward is what the referrer and the new customer receive. The trigger is the event that releases the reward, and for most home services it should be a completed first paid job. The cap is the maximum reward per referrer in a set period. The sample plan proposed a free visit as the reward. That is a United States example from the early 2000s. Before offering any reward in your own business, compare its value with your cost to deliver it.

instruction.heading: Cost the reward per paying customer
instruction.body: Divide the total reward cost in a period by the number of referred customers who completed a first paid job. The result is the cost per referred paying customer, and you can compare it with the cost per new customer from other channels in “Choosing marketing channels and measuring them”. When the reward is paid only after a paid job, and that job is profitable, the reward is a known cost rather than an open promise. The sample plan budgeted its referral incentives as a named line that rose over the period. Its amounts are removed here because they are United States figures. The principle is that a referral line should be budgeted and not left open.

instruction.heading: Consumer and messaging checks
instruction.body: Before a referral scheme goes live, check three things. First, an electronic message that promotes a service can be a commercial electronic message under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). Whether a message a customer forwards on the business's behalf is covered needs a legal reading before you rely on it. Second, reward terms and promotional claims should not mislead customers. Misleading-conduct rules in the Australian Consumer Law may apply, but the ACCC guide cited here does not cover reward terms, so check the current ACL text. Third, some reward or prize schemes may fall under state or territory promotion rules, which differ between states and territories. Check them against current official sources before any scheme goes live, and record the check and its date.

instruction.heading: Do not buy or harvest contacts
instruction.body: Referral messages should only go to people who have agreed to be contacted, or to people a customer has introduced to you with that introduced person's consent. Whether that consent is enough under the Spam Act and privacy rules needs a legal check. Never import a list of contacts to send a reward offer. Buying a list does not free the sender from proving that each person agreed, so do not buy or scrape contact lists. Never create a referral that did not happen in order to claim a reward. A scheme built on harvested contacts is a compliance problem and also damages the trust that referrals depend on.

procedure: Write the reward, the trigger, the cap and the end date on a one-page terms sheet.
Check the terms against the consumer and messaging points in this lesson, and mark each point as confirmed (with a source and date) or leave it out.
Message only people who have consented, or who were introduced with consent. Include sender details and an opt-out in any electronic message.
Log each referral, its first paid job and the reward paid.
Each quarter, divide the total reward cost by the number of referred customers who completed a first paid job.
If the cost per referred paying customer is higher than the value of that customer's first year, change or stop the scheme and record why.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaning team (hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson) offers a $40 AUD credit to any customer whose referred friend completes a first paid job. Over one quarter, 12 referred friends book, 9 complete a first paid job, and the credits paid total $360 AUD.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the reward working, and what should be checked before the next quarter?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cost per referred paying customer is $40 AUD ($360 AUD divided by 9), which equals the reward itself because the trigger is a paid job. Confirm that the three friends who did not complete a paid job were not credited. Compare the $40 AUD figure with the cost per new customer from other channels. Do not extend the offer until the consumer and messaging checks in this lesson are complete and recorded.

commonErrors.error: Paying the reward on a mention or before any paid job
commonErrors.prevention: Make the first completed paid job the payment trigger, and write it into the terms.

commonErrors.error: Sending referral emails or texts to contacts who never agreed
commonErrors.prevention: Message only consenting people, and include sender identification and an opt-out in any electronic message.

commonErrors.error: Launching a scheme with vague terms
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward, trigger, cap and end date in one short sheet that customers can read before they refer.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Spam Act 2003 (Cth): the ACMA guidance summarised in the officialReferences says marketing messages need consent, correct sender details and an unsubscribe option. That guidance does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check the Act for personal referral messages.

Australian Consumer Law (Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2): misleading or deceptive conduct rules apply to advertising. Their application to reward terms is not sourced in this lesson, so check the current ACL text before launch.
State and territory promotion, lottery or prize rules may apply to some reward schemes. Check with the relevant state or territory regulator before launch.
This lesson gives no legal advice and does not grant any licence, registration or authority.

qualityStandard: Referral terms are written and dated, and the customer sees them before referring.
Each reward is paid only on the trigger stated in the terms.
No referral message is sent without a documented consent basis.
documentationEvidence: Log of referrals, first paid jobs and rewards paid
Record of each consumer and messaging check, with its status and source
summary: Pay a reward on a real event, such as a first completed paid job.
Put the reward, trigger, cap and end date in writing.
Check the consumer and messaging rules before launch.

knowledgeChecks.question: Under a sound referral design, when should the reward usually be paid?
options: When the referrer first mentions a friend at the start of the chat
After the new customer completes a paid job, under written terms
Before any job, to secure the friend's commitment and the first bill
Once the referrer has sent the most messages to the friend

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer names a friend who might like the service. What should happen before a referral message is sent?
options: Send it straight away to speed up sales without asking the friend first
Check the consent and sender rules for commercial electronic messages first
Add the friend's address to a purchased list and send the offer to every name
Ask the friend to pay the reward before the job starts for the friend

knowledgeChecks.question: What is a cap on a referral reward?
options: A limit on the number of customers the business can serve each week and each month of the year
A maximum reward per referrer, or a maximum number of rewards, in a set period, written into the terms
A rating the customer gives the business after each job
A colour code used on the booking sheet for each referral

sourceReferences: Cleaning Service Marketing Plan (sample residential cleaning plan, US figures 2002 to 2006), sections Marketing Strategy and Expense Forecast; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying). Referral figures are US and dated; used as method illustration only.
Spam Act 2003 (Cth): summarised from ACMA guidance (officialReferences R1, checked 2026-11-04). The Act text was not read, and coverage of one-to-one messages is not confirmed.

Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2 (Australian Consumer Law): misleading-conduct point for advertising; reward-terms point not checked, and the ACCC guide (R2) does not cover reward terms.
State and territory promotion and prize rules: UNCONFIRMED; not researched in this pass.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: ACMA page: marketing messages need consent from each person who will receive them before sending, need correct sender contact details, and must contain an unsubscribe option that is honoured within 5 working days. The page does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered: remains UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Advertising and selling guide: A guide for business
officialReferences.covers: Advertising guidance: a single advertised price should state the total price, including any mandatory fees and charges. Does not address reward terms or promotion rules, which remain UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: ACCC.
